slides: Open by presenting the chapter as the surface analogue of the curve chapter. A surface is now read through a two-parameter patch, a tangent plane, a metric, and a second-order bending form. Stress that the deck follows the notebook artifacts and the assigned source span, while using original diagrams and computed checks rather than scanned page material.

Use the parameter patch as the first mental model. The surface is not studied all at once; it is locally sampled by two independent coordinate directions. Point out the pole warning on the sphere: a coordinate failure changes the metric determinant even though the underlying surface remains perfectly regular.

Emphasize that tangent vectors on a surface are measured by the metric, not by the raw coordinate coefficients. The same geometric tangent direction has contravariant components, covariant components, and a unit condition given by an ellipse in coefficient space. That is why tensor notation enters naturally here.

Frame normal curvature as the bridge from tangent measurement to bending measurement. The numerator uses the second fundamental form and the denominator uses the first fundamental form, so the quotient compares two quadratic forms on the same direction. Rotating the direction gives a full scan of sectional bending.

Present principal curvatures as an optimization result, not as mysterious named quantities. The maximum and minimum normal curvatures occur when the Rayleigh quotient is stationary, which produces the generalized eigenproblem. The displayed checks show that the two eigen-directions are orthogonal in the surface metric.

Use the three panels as a local taxonomy. Positive Gaussian curvature bends the same way in every normal section, zero Gaussian curvature has a flat normal-section direction, and negative Gaussian curvature has opposite signs. The determinant formula makes this classification independent of the chosen coordinates.

Separate the idea of positive curvature from the idea of an umbilic. A sphere is umbilic everywhere because the two principal curvatures agree, but many positively curved surfaces still have preferred principal directions. The surface-of-revolution plot makes this distinction visible by comparing the sphere with an ordinary spheroid.

Explain Dupin's theorem through the concrete orthogonal systems in the artifact. Three mutually orthogonal families give curvature lines on each member because the orthogonality condition forces both the metric cross term and the mixed second fundamental coefficient to vanish. The proof map is included to keep the logic inspectable.

Treat Liouville's theorem as the conformal companion to Dupin's theorem. Inversion is the model transformation: it preserves sampled angles and sends a plane not through the origin to a sphere. The numerical residuals demonstrate sphere preservation and angle preservation without relying on a copied textbook figure.

Close with Dupin's indicatrix as the compression of the whole chapter. The tangent-plane conic records all normal curvatures through Euler's formula, distinguishing elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic local behavior. The applied lab then changes the quadratic form directly, showing how principal curvatures, mean curvature, and Gaussian curvature move together.
